questions.stem: Laws on the non-consensual sharing of intimate images were introduced after smartphones and social media made such sharing easy. Which reason for change does this best show?
options: Amending an outdated law
Recognising changing values
Adapting to technological change
Upholding international standards
questions.explanation: New technology created conduct that existing laws did not clearly cover, so new offences were needed. Changing values can also play a part, but the trigger here was the technology itself.

questions.stem: In 2019 NSW removed abortion from the Crimes Act 1900 and regulated it as a health matter. Which reason for law reform does this most clearly show?
options: Implementing a ruling of an international court
Responding to a decision of the High Court
Recognising changing values in society
Adapting to developments in technology
questions.explanation: The Abortion Law Reform Act 2019 (NSW) reflected changed community attitudes towards abortion as a health and personal matter. It was not required by any court decision.

questions.stem: Australia ratifies a treaty and then passes legislation so that domestic law meets its obligations. Which reason for change is this?
options: Maintaining relevance in society
Adapting to technological change
Addressing a single person's needs
Upholding international standards
questions.explanation: Ratified treaties often require domestic legislation, as with the Racial Discrimination Act 1975, which gave effect to an international convention. Australia's dualist system means the treaty alone does not change domestic law.

questions.stem: In 2014 NSW created the offence of assault causing death after single-punch attacks in Sydney. Which statement best explains the reason for this reform?
options: New technology had made single-punch assaults possible for the first time in Australia's history
The High Court had declared the offence of manslaughter invalid, leaving a gap in the criminal law
Existing offences were seen as failing to meet society's need for protection from a particular type of violence
An international court ordered NSW to create the offence after a complaint from another country
questions.explanation: Public concern after deaths from single punches led the government to argue that existing laws did not adequately address this conduct, so section 25A was added to the Crimes Act 1900. No court or treaty required the change, and manslaughter remains an offence.

questions.stem: A law that no longer serves any purpose because the conduct it regulated has disappeared is repealed. Which reason for change does this best show?
options: Adapting to developments in new technology
Responding to an international court ruling
Amending existing or outdated laws
Upholding international standards for human rights
questions.explanation: Statute books contain laws that become obsolete or out of step with society, and repealing or updating them keeps the law clear and relevant. No technology or international obligation is involved in this example.

questions.stem: A government changes the law so that people with disability can more easily access public buildings and services. Which reason for law reform does this mainly show?
options: Overturning a decision of the High Court of Australia
Maintaining the stability of the law by keeping it unchanged
Addressing the needs of a particular group in society
Adapting to technological change in the building industry
questions.explanation: Reform often responds to the needs of individuals or groups whose rights or interests are not adequately protected. Changing the law here is about meeting a group's needs, not responding to a court or technology.

questions.stem: Which is an informal method of influencing law reform?
options: A NSW Law Reform Commission report to the Attorney General
A High Court decision overruling an earlier precedent
A media campaign drawing attention to a gap in the law
A bill being passed by both houses of the NSW Parliament
questions.explanation: Informal methods, such as media campaigns, protests, petitions and lobbying, try to persuade decision-makers but cannot change the law themselves. Parliament, law reform commissions and the courts are formal mechanisms.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the difference between activism and advocacy as drivers of law reform?
options: Activism changes the law immediately once a protest occurs; advocacy has no effect unless a court agrees
Activism is a formal method of reform; advocacy is an informal method used only by the news media
Activism usually involves direct public action such as protests; advocacy involves arguing a case to decision-makers
Activism can only be carried out by members of parliament; advocacy can only be carried out by judges sitting in court
questions.explanation: Activists use visible action such as marches, campaigns and civil disobedience to build pressure, while advocates, including NGOs and peak bodies, make submissions and lobby. Both are informal drivers of change.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant limitation of public opinion as a driver of law reform?
options: It can be divided or short-lived, and laws made quickly in response to outrage may be poorly designed
It has no influence on governments, because members of parliament never consider voters' views
It can only be expressed through a referendum, which must be held before any law can be changed
It must be approved by the High Court before parliament is allowed to consider it in any debate
questions.explanation: Governments respond to public opinion, but opinion is often split, influenced by media coverage and quick to move on, and reactive laws can have unintended effects. Parliament can change most laws without a referendum.

questions.stem: A family whose son was killed starts a campaign, gives media interviews and meets the Attorney General to push for tougher laws. What does this best show?
options: Individuals have no role in law reform, which is only carried out by law reform bodies
Individuals can drive reform by attracting public attention and lobbying decision-makers
Individuals can change the law directly by signing a statement with the Attorney General
Individuals can only influence the law by becoming members of the NSW Parliament
questions.explanation: Personal campaigns can put an issue on the political agenda, but parliament must still pass any change. Many reforms began with campaigns by victims' families.

questions.stem: Which is the main strength of the media as a driver of law reform?
options: It always presents every side of an issue fairly, so its influence is never biased
It can pass laws in an emergency when parliament is not sitting during the year
It can rapidly raise awareness and put pressure on governments to respond to an issue
It can make binding recommendations that the government must then turn into legislation
questions.explanation: Investigative journalism and social media can expose problems and mobilise public opinion. The media's coverage can also be sensational or one-sided, and it has no law-making power.

questions.stem: The NSW Law Reform Commission is best described as:
options: a committee of members of parliament that votes on whether bills should become law in NSW
a royal commission set up to investigate misconduct by government agencies and public officials
an independent body that investigates areas of law referred by the Attorney General and recommends changes
a court that can strike down NSW laws it finds unjust after hearing arguments from the community
questions.explanation: The NSW Law Reform Commission, established under the Law Reform Commission Act 1967 (NSW), researches, consults and reports on references from the Attorney General. Its recommendations are not binding on parliament.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates law reform commissions as formal agents of change?
options: They are elected by voters, so their reports carry more democratic legitimacy than acts of parliament
Their research and consultation produce well-considered proposals, but governments may ignore or delay them
Their recommendations become law automatically once the commission tables its final report in the parliament
They respond to public outrage within days, which makes them the fastest way to change the law in NSW
questions.explanation: Commissions are independent and thorough, consulting widely before recommending change. Their reports can take years, and implementation depends on the government's political will.

questions.stem: Which feature most clearly distinguishes a royal commission from a law reform commission?
options: A royal commission can sentence people it finds have broken the law during its investigation
A royal commission is permanent and investigates any area of law the public suggests to it
A royal commission can pass legislation once its recommendations have been made public
A royal commission has coercive powers to compel witnesses and documents in a public inquiry
questions.explanation: Royal commissions are temporary inquiries with strong powers to compel evidence, which suits investigating systemic failures. They cannot convict or legislate; they report and recommend.

questions.stem: In 2021 a NSW parliamentary committee inquired into coercive control, and an offence of coercive control in intimate relationships began on 1 July 2024. Which formal method of change began this process?
options: A special commission of inquiry
A referendum
A parliamentary inquiry
A High Court decision
questions.explanation: A Joint Select Committee of the NSW Parliament examined coercive control and recommended criminalising it, and Parliament later legislated. Parliamentary inquiries let members hear evidence directly from the community and experts.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares parliamentary inquiries with royal commissions as drivers of law reform?
options: Inquiries have stronger powers to compel evidence than royal commissions, but they are far more expensive to run
Inquiries can make binding orders against individuals, while royal commissions can only make recommendations
Inquiries are run by judges appointed for life, while royal commissions are run by members of the government
Inquiries are cheaper and linked directly to parliament, but they may be influenced by party politics and lack coercive powers
questions.explanation: Parliamentary committees are inexpensive and can feed directly into legislation, but members may divide along party lines. Royal commissions are independent and powerful but costly and slower.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a legislative process of law reform?
options: A royal commission tabling its final report in the NSW parliament
Parliament passing a bill that amends the Crimes Act 1900 (NSW)
A court interpreting the words of an Act in a new case
A minister approving a regulation under an existing Act
questions.explanation: Legislative reform happens when parliament passes, amends or repeals an Act. Making a regulation under an Act is an executive process, and courts change the law through judicial decisions.

questions.stem: NSW decriminalised abortion in 2019 and legalised voluntary assisted dying in 2022 through bills introduced by an individual member of parliament, with members allowed to vote according to conscience. Such bills are called:
options: government money bills
delegated legislation
royal commission bills
private members' bills
questions.explanation: A private member's bill is introduced by a member who is not a minister, and conscience votes free members from voting along party lines. These bills show how parliament can reform laws on contested moral issues.

questions.stem: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the NSW Health Minister made public health orders under the Public Health Act 2010 (NSW). Which process of change does this show?
options: An executive method, using power delegated by parliament
A judicial method, using the doctrine of binding precedent
A legislative method, by passing a new Act
An informal method, through a media campaign
questions.explanation: The executive can change rules quickly by using powers that an Act gives a minister, such as orders and regulations. Such delegated powers can be scrutinised by parliament and challenged in court.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a judicial process of law reform?
options: The Governor issuing letters patent to establish a new royal commission
A minister making a regulation that sets new fees for a government licence
The High Court overruling earlier authority and recognising a new common law right
Parliament passing an amendment after a law reform commission report has been tabled
questions.explanation: Courts change the common law through precedent and shape statute law through interpretation, as in Mabo (No 2). Establishing a royal commission and making regulations are executive actions.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains a limitation of courts as agents of law reform?
options: Courts can change any law at any time on their own initiative, which makes their reforms both undemocratic and frequent
Courts must hold a public vote before changing the common law, which makes judicial reform slow and expensive
Courts cannot interpret legislation in any way, so they have no influence on the meaning of statute law
Courts can only decide the cases brought before them and must defer to parliament, which can override their decisions
questions.explanation: Judicial change depends on a suitable case reaching court, it is bound by precedent, and parliament can legislate to change a judicial decision. Courts cannot start reforms on their own initiative.

questions.stem: Which is a benefit of successful law reform?
options: The law applies only to the people who campaigned for it
The law better reflects community values and meets society's needs
The law becomes fixed, so it never has to be changed again
The law no longer needs to be enforced by police or courts
questions.explanation: Effective reform keeps the law relevant and fair, improving public confidence and protecting rights. Laws continue to need review and enforcement after reform.

questions.stem: A new offence is created after public outrage, but courts later find it hard to apply and few prosecutions succeed. Which limitation of law reform does this best show?
options: Reform always leads to more prosecutions, so a low number shows the new law is working
Reform cannot happen without a referendum, so the offence was never valid
Reform must be approved by an international court before it can be enforced
Rushed reform can produce laws that are poorly drafted and fail to achieve their aim
questions.explanation: Reform made quickly without careful research or consultation may contain gaps or unintended effects. This is why many argue for careful review by bodies such as law reform commissions.

questions.stem: Which is a common limitation of law reform even when a new law is well designed?
options: It cannot apply to anyone who was born before the date on which it was passed
Lack of funding, awareness or enforcement can stop it achieving its intended outcome
It automatically repeals every other law that deals with the same topic in NSW
It can be challenged only in an international court, so it can never be reviewed locally
questions.explanation: A law's effectiveness depends on resources, enforcement and public understanding, not just its wording. Without support services or police training, reform may change little in practice.

questions.stem: Which NSW Act established the NSW Aboriginal Land Council and a network of Local Aboriginal Land Councils?
options: The Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW)
The Real Property Act 1900 (NSW)
The Aboriginal Land Rights Act 1983 (NSW)
The Native Title Act 1993 (Cth)
questions.explanation: The Aboriginal Land Rights Act 1983 (NSW) set up land councils and allowed them to claim certain Crown land. The Native Title Act 1993 is a Commonwealth Act that followed the Mabo decision.

questions.stem: Under the Aboriginal Land Rights Act 1983 (NSW), Aboriginal Land Councils can claim land that is:
options: only land that the High Court has already found to be subject to native title in a court decision
claimable Crown land, such as land not lawfully used or occupied and not needed for an essential public purpose
any privately owned freehold land in NSW, whatever the wishes of the person who currently owns it
land in any Australian state or territory, because the Act applies across the whole Commonwealth
questions.explanation: Successful claims transfer claimable Crown land to the land council as freehold. Private freehold land cannot be claimed, and the Act applies only in NSW.

questions.stem: What is the main legal difference between statutory land rights in NSW and native title?
options: Land rights are granted by legislation, while native title is the recognition of rights that existed before British settlement
Land rights are recognised only by the common law, while native title is granted to land councils by the NSW Parliament
Land rights apply only to land in the Northern Territory, while native title applies only to land in New South Wales
Land rights can never be sold or leased, while native title is ordinary freehold that can be sold to anyone
questions.explanation: Land rights involve parliament granting land, usually as freehold to land councils. Native title is the common law's recognition of continuing rights and interests under traditional laws and customs, which must be proved.

questions.stem: The doctrine of terra nullius, overturned in Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992), held that Australia at British settlement was:
options: land subject to native title
land belonging to no one
land held in trust by the Crown
land shared equally by treaty
questions.explanation: Terra nullius treated the continent as if no one owned it, ignoring Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples' relationship with land. The High Court rejected it as a basis of Australian property law in Mabo (No 2).

questions.stem: In Milirrpum v Nabalco (1971), the Yolngu people challenged bauxite mining on the Gove Peninsula. What did the Supreme Court of the Northern Territory decide?
options: It refused to recognise communal native title, applying the doctrine that Australia had been settled
It recognised native title for the first time and ordered the mining company to leave the land
It held that the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 made the mining leases invalid from the beginning
It referred the case to the International Court of Justice because it involved Indigenous peoples
questions.explanation: Justice Blackburn found that the claimants had a system of law but that communal native title was not part of Australian law. The decision was a driver of change: it led to the Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976 and was later overtaken by Mabo (No 2).

questions.stem: In Mabo v Queensland (No 1) (1988), the High Court found a Queensland Act that tried to extinguish the Meriam people's claimed rights was invalid. Why?
options: It had been passed without a referendum, which the Constitution requires for all laws about land
It breached the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth), which had already been passed by the federal Parliament in Canberra
It conflicted with a UN declaration that applies directly in Australian courts without legislation
It was inconsistent with the Racial Discrimination Act 1975 (Cth), so it was invalid under section 109
questions.explanation: The Queensland Coast Islands Declaratory Act 1985 treated the Meriam people's property rights less favourably than others', so it conflicted with the Racial Discrimination Act and was invalid under section 109. The Native Title Act did not yet exist.

questions.stem: What did the High Court decide in Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992)?
options: Native title can be recognised only after the Commonwealth Parliament passes a law creating it
Native title survived the Crown's acquisition of sovereignty where it had not been extinguished
The Crown never acquired sovereignty over the Murray Islands, so Queensland law does not apply
All land in Australia is held under native title, so freehold titles granted since 1788 are invalid
questions.explanation: By a majority of six to one, the Court held that the Meriam people held native title to the Murray Islands and that native title exists where it has not been extinguished, for example by a grant of freehold. Sovereignty and existing freehold titles were not overturned.

questions.stem: Which Act did the Commonwealth Parliament pass in response to Mabo (No 2) to set up a process for recognising native title?
options: The Real Property Act 1900
The Racial Discrimination Act 1975
The Native Title Act 1993
The Land Rights Act 1983
questions.explanation: The Native Title Act 1993 (Cth), which commenced on 1 January 1994, set up the National Native Title Tribunal and a process for claims to be determined by the Federal Court. It also validated past grants of land.

questions.stem: What did the High Court decide in Wik Peoples v Queensland (1996)?
options: Pastoral leases did not necessarily extinguish native title, which could coexist with them
Pastoral leases were invalid and had to be returned to the traditional owners of the land
Native title was extinguished on all land in Queensland that had ever been used for farming
Native title claims could be decided only by the National Native Title Tribunal, not courts
questions.explanation: By four to three, the Court held that native title could coexist with pastoral leases, but where the rights conflicted, the pastoralist's rights prevailed. The decision led to political debate and the Native Title Amendment Act 1998.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the effect of the Native Title Amendment Act 1998 (Cth)?
options: It responded to Wik by confirming extinguishment on some tenures and restricting the right to negotiate
It extended native title to all privately owned freehold land in Australia in response to the Wik decision
It abolished native title entirely and replaced it with state land rights schemes in every state
It made native title claims easier by removing the need to prove any connection to the land
questions.explanation: The 1998 amendments, based on the government's ten-point plan, gave certainty to pastoralists and governments but were criticised for reducing native title holders' rights. They also introduced Indigenous Land Use Agreements.

questions.stem: In Members of the Yorta Yorta Aboriginal Community v Victoria (2002), the High Court rejected a native title claim. What does the case show about a limitation of native title law?
options: Claimants must prove a continuing connection with the land under traditional laws and customs since sovereignty
Native title can only be claimed by people who lived on the land before the year 1901 and are still alive
Native title claims must be approved by a referendum in the state where the land is located
Native title claims can only be made over land that has been granted as freehold since 1788
questions.explanation: The Court required continuous acknowledgment and observance of traditional laws and customs, which is very hard to prove where dispossession disrupted connection. This shows how the burden of proof limits native title as a remedy.

questions.stem: Which is a benefit that has resulted from native title law?
options: Native title has returned all Crown and private land in Australia to its traditional owners
Native title has ended the need for any land rights legislation in New South Wales
Native title allows claimants to cancel any mining lease granted over their land since 1788
Agreements such as Indigenous Land Use Agreements give traditional owners a voice in how land is used
questions.explanation: Native title determinations and agreements have recognised rights and given traditional owners negotiating power over activities on their land. Native title is extinguished by freehold and does not override validly granted interests.
